EMNLP 2023Learning from new knowledge

ALCUNA: Large Language Models Meet New Knowledge

Xunjian Yin1*, Baizhou Huang1*, Xiaojun Wan1

1 Peking University · * Equal contribution

Paper ↗arXiv ↗Code ↗Data ↗

ALCUNA creates fictional organisms to test knowledge that models have not memorized, exposing a gap between reading new facts and connecting them to existing knowledge.

Result
ChatGPT, the strongest tested model, scores 75.44% on knowledge understanding but 41.52% on knowledge association (few-shot vanilla); all four models score lowest on association there.
New vs prior
Temporal benchmarks such as TemporalWiki must be recollected and may leak into training data, and entity substitution (Longpre et al., 2022) builds contradicting statements; this work generates ontology-consistent artificial entities.
Limitation
KnowGen is implemented only on biological taxonomy data, and only four 2023 models (ChatGPT, Alpaca-7B, Vicuna-13B, ChatGLM-6B) are evaluated.
01 / The research question

Artificial entities make novelty verifiable

A correct answer about a new entity may come from memorization, from the supplied description, or from a guess prompted by a familiar name. ALCUNA controls for memorization by construction: its generator, KnowGen, creates artificial organisms by transforming entities in the Encyclopedia of Life (EOL) taxonomy, so every property traces back to a known operation.

Properties shared by the class are kept while selected attributes and relations change, so the questions stay biologically meaningful. This is a harder test than an arbitrary name with unrelated facts: the new entity resembles one the model already knows, so familiar knowledge can support reasoning or interfere with the new description.

Closest prior work

Earlier evaluations obtain new knowledge from temporal change, as in TemporalWiki (Jang et al., 2023) and Lazaridou et al. (2021); the paper notes that such data must be recollected for each new model, may already be in undisclosed training data, and differs across models with different cutoffs. Entity-substitution methods (Longpre et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023) replace an entity name in a short statement to create knowledge that contradicts the model. KnowGen instead builds a complete artificial entity in ontological form, through heredity, variation, extension, and dropout, so the new knowledge stays consistent with, and connected to, existing knowledge.

02 / Inside the method

Each KnowGen operation fixes an expected answer

KnowGen starts from a parent entity and its siblings in the same class. Heredity keeps a parent property, variation perturbs a numeric value or swaps in a value from a related entity, extension adds a sibling's property, and dropout removes a parent property. Each operation fixes the expected answer to a question.

  • Heredity keeps a parent property unchanged.
  • Variation perturbs a value: Gaussian noise for a number, a sibling of the related entity for a relation.
  • Dropout removes a parent property from the new entity.
  • Extension adds a property sampled from a sibling of the parent.

Example: Figure 1, Algorithm 1, and Sections 2.3–2.4 of the EMNLP 2023 paper. With all four operations on, the entity and the five questions are exactly those printed in Figure 1. Other switch settings apply Algorithm 1's rules to the same printed properties; their question sets and answers are derived here and labelled so. KD questions come from varied and dropped attributes, KA questions from relation chains found by breadth-first search, and KU questions from the remaining properties (Section 2.4). The real benchmark has 11.75 property triplets per entity on average; Figure 1 prints five.

Differentiation questions target the varied and dropped properties. Asked for a lifespan that dropout removed, the correct answer is that it is unknown, even though the parent's lifespan is easy to recall. Association questions follow a relation from the artificial entity into existing knowledge and finish the chain with a fact absent from the new description.

Questions are filtered so that each model fully recalls the parent entity and every hop of a reasoning chain, and the intersection across models is used. A failure therefore points to combining facts, not to a missing prerequisite.

  1. 01

    Create unfamiliar entities

    KnowGen modifies attributes and relations in biological taxonomy data to generate artificial organisms with controlled connections to real entities.

  2. 02

    Separate three abilities

    Evaluate understanding, differentiation, and association with questions that require progressively more interaction between supplied facts and existing knowledge.

  3. 03

    Vary the context

    Compare prompting settings, entity similarity, and additional context to identify where models confuse or fail to connect knowledge.

03 / Reading the evidence

The bottleneck is linking new to existing knowledge

  • 75.44 vs 41.52

    ChatGPT: understanding vs association (%)

    Few-shot vanilla accuracy. The strongest model reads the new entity's description well but struggles to connect it to knowledge it already has.

  • 27.47 → 44.43

    ChatGLM association with chain entities (%)

    Adding the entities on the reasoning chain to the context raises association; the same number of irrelevant entities lowers it to 18.56.

The context ablations show why separate ability scores matter. Supplying the chain entities raises association for all three open models, so the main problem is linking new and existing knowledge, not only multi-hop reasoning. Adding the parent entity instead lowers Vicuna's differentiation from 46.76 to 35.04: related context can supply a missing link or strengthen the wrong association.

Presentation also matters. All three open models score higher when the new entity is given as structured JSON than as natural-language text; ChatGLM's average falls to 20.54 with natural language. Success therefore depends partly on how new knowledge is communicated.

Read the abstract

With the rapid development of NLP, large-scale language models (LLMs) excel in various tasks across multiple domains now. However, existing benchmarks may not adequately measure these models’ capabilities, especially when faced with new knowledge. In this paper, we address the lack of benchmarks to evaluate LLMs’ ability to handle new knowledge, an important and challenging aspect in the rapidly evolving world. We propose an approach called KnowGen that generates new knowledge by altering existing entity attributes and relationships, resulting in artificial entities that are distinct from real-world entities. With KnowGen, we introduce a benchmark named ALCUNA to assess LLMs’ abilities in knowledge understanding, differentiation, and association. We benchmark several LLMs, reveals that their performance in face of new knowledge is not satisfactory, particularly in reasoning between new and internal knowledge. We also explore the impact of entity similarity on the model’s understanding of entity knowledge and the influence of contextual entities. We appeal to the need for caution when using LLMs in new scenarios or with new knowledge, and hope that our benchmarks can help drive the development of LLMs in face of new knowledge.
